title: The nonsense question
translation: There was a man called Suketsue, I think, a senior counsellor who had become a lay monk. One day he said to Tomouji, a captain in the palace guards: "Ask me anything you like. Whatever it is, I'll have an answer."
"I never studied anything serious, not even a little, so there's no point asking you about that. I'll ask you about some bit of nonsense I've never understood."
"Even better. Small everyday things? I'll explain anything."

The courtiers and the ladies of the palace loved it. "What a fun contest. Do it in front of the emperor. And whoever loses pays for a feast for him." So it was settled, and the two of them faced each other before the emperor.
Tomouji said: "I've heard this since I was a child, and I've never known what it means. Uma no kitsuryō kitsuni no oka nakakubo reiri gurendō. What does it mean? Please tell me."
Suketsue was stuck. "That's nonsense. It isn't worth talking about."
"I never said I knew anything deep. We agreed I'd ask you about nonsense."
So Suketsue lost, and the feast he had to give was a very grand one.

{具氏|ともうぢ}、「いかが{侍|はべ}らむ。」と{申|まう}されけるを、「さらば、あらがひ{給|たま}へ。」といはれて、
「はかばかしき{事|こと}は、{片端|かたはし}もまねび{知|し}り{侍|はべ}らねば、{尋|たづ}ね{申|まう}すまでもなし。{何|なに}となきそぞろごとの{中|なか}に、{覚束|おぼつか}なき{事|こと}をこそ{問|と}ひ{奉|たてまつ}らめ。」と{申|まう}されけり。
「まして、ここもとの{浅|あさ}きことは、{何事|なにごと}なりともあきらめ{申|まう}さむ。」といはれければ、
{近習|きんじふ}の{人々|ひとびと}、{女房|にようばう}なども、「{興|きよう}あるあらがひなり。おなじくは{御前|ごぜん}にて{争|あらそ}はるべし。{負|ま}けたらむ{人|ひと}は{供御|ぐご}をまうけらるべし。」と{定|さだ}めて、{御前|ごぜん}にて{召|め}し{合|あは}せられたりけるに、
{具氏|ともうぢ}、「{幼|をさな}くより{聞|き}きならひ{侍|はべ}れど、その{心|こころ}{知|し}らぬこと{侍|はべ}り。{馬|うま}のきつりやうきつにのをか、なかくぼれいりぐれんどうと{申|まう}すことは、いかなる{心|こころ}にかはべらむ。{承|うけたまは}らむ。」と{申|まう}されけるに、
{大納言|だいなごん}{入道|にふだう}はたとつまりて、「これは、そぞろごとなれば、{云|い}ふにも{足|た}らず。」といはれけるを、
「もとより、{深|ふか}き{道|みち}は{知|し}り{侍|はべ}らず。そぞろ{言|ごと}を{尋|たづ}ね{奉|たてまつ}らむと、{定|さだ}め{申|まう}しつ。」と{申|まう}されければ、
{大納言|だいなごん}{入道|にふだう}{負|ま}けになりて、{所課|しよくわ}いかめしくせられたりけるとぞ。
literal: A person who was called, I think, the Major Counsellor and lay monk Suketsue met the Consultant and Middle Captain Tomouji and said, 'Whatever thing you may ask, would I not answer it?', and when he said this,
Tomouji said, 'How would that be?', to which (Suketsue) said, 'Then dispute it', and (Tomouji said):
'Since I have not learned even a scrap of serious things, there is no need to ask about them. Among meaningless trifles, I shall ask you about something I am unsure of.' So he said.
'All the more, shallow matters close at hand, whatever they are, I will explain', (Suketsue) said, and

the attendants and the court ladies too decided: 'It is an amusing dispute. If you are going to, contest it before His Majesty. Whoever loses must provide a meal for His Majesty', and when they were matched against each other before His Majesty,

Tomouji said: 'I have heard it since I was young, but there is something whose meaning I do not know. What is the meaning of what is called "uma no kitsuryō kitsuni no oka nakakubo reiri gurendō"? I would like to hear it.'
The Major Counsellor lay monk was stuck short and said, 'This is a trifle, so it is not even worth speaking of', to which
(Tomouji) said, 'From the start, I do not know deep matters. I settled that I would ask you about trifles', and so
the Major Counsellor lay monk lost, and they say the forfeit he provided was grand.

notes.text: Fujiwara no Suketsue (died 1289, aged 83), a court noble who rose to Major Counsellor ({大納言|だいなごん}) and later took Buddhist vows while living at home ({入道|にふだう}, 'lay monk'). The 1925 edition identifies him as the son of Sukeie. とかや: 'I think he was called', a hedge on the name.

Minamoto no Tomouji (died 1275, aged 44), son of Michiuji (so the 1925 edition), about twenty-five years younger than Suketsue. {宰相|さいしやう} is another name for a Consultant on the council of state, {中将|ちゆうじやう} a Middle Captain of the palace guards.
'You', familiar and a little condescending. Suketsue talks down to Tomouji from the first word.
や here is rhetorical: 'would I not answer? (Of course I would.)'
あらがふ: 'to dispute, to challenge', and so 'to bet'.

notes.quote: 負けたらむ人は供御をまうけらるべし
notes.text: {供御|ぐご}: food served to the emperor (or a retired emperor). The text does not say which emperor this was. So the loser does not just lose face: he pays for a royal meal.

notes.quote: 馬のきつりやうきつにのをか、なかくぼれいりぐれんどう
notes.text: Nobody knows what this means, and it may have been made up to mean nothing. The 1925 edition follows a solution by Nunami Keion that reads it as a riddle: 'the horse (うまのきつ) leaves' (take away those five kana); 'the middle sinks in' (of りやうきつにのをか keep only the first り and the last か); 'tumble over' (りか becomes かり, {雁|かり}, 'wild goose'). It is one guess among several. Either way, the trap is in the bet itself: Suketsue had promised to explain nonsense too.
はたと: 'suddenly, with a snap'. つまる: 'to be stuck for an answer'. Modern ことばに{詰|つ}まる is the same verb.

notes.quote: 所課いかめしくせられたりけるとぞ
notes.text: {所課|しよくわ}: the forfeit he was charged with (the edition: 'a feast as a fine'). いかめし: 'grand, imposing'. とぞ: 'so they say', with the verb of saying left out.
